# Functions used below

def dict_to_html(d):
    """Convert a Python dictionary into a two column table for display.
    """

    html = []

    html.append(f'<table width="100%" style="width:100%; font-family: monospace;">')
    for k, v in d.items():
        html.append(f'<tr><td style="text-align:left;">{k}</td><td>{v}</td></tr>')
    html.append(f'</table>')

    return ''.join(html)


def show_as_html(df, n=20):
    """Leverage existing pandas jupyter integration to show a spark dataframe as html.
    
    Args:
        n (int): number of rows to show (default: 20)
    """

    display(df.limit(n).toPandas())

    
def display_spark():
    """Display the status of the active Spark session if one is currently running.
    """
    
    if 'spark' in globals() and 'sc' in globals():

        name = sc.getConf().get("spark.app.name")

        html = [
            f'<p><b>Spark</b></p>',
            f'<p>The spark session is <b><span style="color:green">active</span></b>, look for <code>{name}</code> under the running applications section in the Spark UI.</p>',
            f'<ul>',
            f'<li><a href="http://localhost:{sc.uiWebUrl.split(":")[-1]}" target="_blank">Spark Application UI</a></li>',
            f'</ul>',
            f'<p><b>Config</b></p>',
            dict_to_html(dict(sc.getConf().getAll())),
            f'<p><b>Notes</b></p>',
            f'<ul>',
            f'<li>The spark session <code>spark</code> and spark context <code>sc</code> global variables have been defined by <code>start_spark()</code>.</li>',
            f'<li>Please run <code>stop_spark()</code> before closing the notebook or restarting the kernel or kill <code>{name}</code> by hand using the link in the Spark UI.</li>',
            f'</ul>',
        ]
        display(HTML(''.join(html)))
        
    else:
        
        html = [
            f'<p><b>Spark</b></p>',
            f'<p>The spark session is <b><span style="color:red">stopped</span></b>, confirm that <code>{username} (notebook)</code> is under the completed applications section in the Spark UI.</p>',
            f'<ul>',
            f'<li><a href="http://mathmadslinux2p.canterbury.ac.nz:8080/" target="_blank">Spark UI</a></li>',
            f'</ul>',
        ]
        display(HTML(''.join(html)))


# Functions to start and stop spark

def start_spark(executor_instances=2, executor_cores=1, worker_memory=1, master_memory=1):
    """Start a new Spark session and define globals for SparkSession (spark) and SparkContext (sc).
    
    Args:
        executor_instances (int): number of executors (default: 2)
        executor_cores (int): number of cores per executor (default: 1)
        worker_memory (float): worker memory (default: 1)
        master_memory (float): master memory (default: 1)
    """

    global spark
    global sc

    cores = executor_instances * executor_cores
    partitions = cores * 4
    port = 4000 + random.randint(1, 999)

    spark = (
        SparkSession.builder
        .config("spark.driver.extraJavaOptions", f"-Dderby.system.home=/tmp/{username}/spark/")
        .config("spark.dynamicAllocation.enabled", "false")
        .config("spark.executor.instances", str(executor_instances))
        .config("spark.executor.cores", str(executor_cores))
        .config("spark.cores.max", str(cores))
        .config("spark.driver.memory", f'{master_memory}g')
        .config("spark.executor.memory", f'{worker_memory}g')
        .config("spark.driver.maxResultSize", "0")
        .config("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", str(partitions))
        .config("spark.kubernetes.container.image", "madsregistry001.azurecr.io/hadoop-spark:v3.3.5-openjdk-8")
        .config("spark.kubernetes.container.image.pullPolicy", "IfNotPresent")
        .config("spark.kubernetes.memoryOverheadFactor", "0.3")
        .config("spark.memory.fraction", "0.1")
        .config(f"fs.azure.sas.{azure_user_container_name}.{azure_account_name}.blob.core.windows.net",  azure_user_token)
        .config("spark.app.name", f"{username} (notebook)")
        .getOrCreate()
    )
    sc = SparkContext.getOrCreate()
    
    display_spark()

    
def stop_spark():
    """Stop the active Spark session and delete globals for SparkSession (spark) and SparkContext (sc).
    """

    global spark
    global sc

    if 'spark' in globals() and 'sc' in globals():

        spark.stop()

        del spark
        del sc

    display_spark()

Finding the actual missing date¶

In [34]:
from pyspark.sql.functions import sequence, explode

all_dates = (
    date_range
    .select(
        explode(
            sequence(
                col("MIN_DATE"),
                col("MAX_DATE")
            )
        ).alias("DATE")
    )
)

actual_dates = (
    nz_tmin_tmax
    .select(
        to_date(col("DATE"), "yyyyMMdd").alias("DATE")
    )
    .distinct()
)
missing_dates = (
    all_dates
    .join(
        actual_dates,
        on="DATE",
        how="left_anti"
    )
    .orderBy("DATE")
)

The important point is that we're not saying individual stations have complete coverage. We're saying that on these 44 dates, there was no TMIN/TMAX observation anywhere among the NZ stations in our filtered dataset.

Q1(a) — Final results
Question	                    Result
Total TMIN/TMAX observations	500,840
Years covered	                87 years
Period covered	                1940–2026
First observation	            1940-03-08
Last observation	            2026-08-01
Expected calendar days	        31,558
Actual dates with observations	31,514
Dates with no observations	    44

Question 1(a): Answer¶

There are 500,840 TMIN and TMAX observations for New Zealand stations, covering 87 years from 1940 to 2026. The observations range from 8 March 1940 to 1 August 2026. There are 44 dates with no TMIN or TMAX observations reported by any of the NZ stations, so there are some gaps in the data.

Aggregating to monthly averages¶

In [37]:
from pyspark.sql.functions import date_trunc, avg

nz_monthly = (
    nz_climate_clean
    .withColumn(
        "YEAR_MONTH",
        date_trunc("month", col("DATE"))
    )
    .withColumn(
        "TEMP_C",
        col("VALUE") / 10
    )
    .groupBy(
        "ID",
        "YEAR_MONTH",
        "ELEMENT"
    )
    .agg(
        avg("TEMP_C").alias("AVG_TEMP_C")
    )
    .orderBy(
        "ID",
        "YEAR_MONTH",
        "ELEMENT"
    )
)

nz_monthly.show(20, truncate=False)

Reshaping Data for Plotting¶

In [38]:
from pyspark.sql.functions import first

nz_monthly_wide = (
    nz_monthly
    .groupBy("ID", "YEAR_MONTH")
    .pivot("ELEMENT", ["TMIN", "TMAX"])
    .agg(first("AVG_TEMP_C"))
    .orderBy("ID", "YEAR_MONTH")
)

nz_monthly_wide.printSchema()
nz_monthly_wide.show(20, truncate=False)

    f"@{azure_account_name}.blob.core.windows.net/"
    f"{username}"
)

    NZ_MONTHLY_OUTPUT
)

Creating monthly timeline for each station¶

In [11]:
# Create the complete monthly timeline
full_months = pd.date_range(
    start=nz_monthly_pd["YEAR_MONTH"].min(),
    end=nz_monthly_pd["YEAR_MONTH"].max(),
    freq="MS"
)

print("Total months in complete timeline:", len(full_months))
print("Start:", full_months.min())
print("End:", full_months.max())

Total months in complete timeline: 1038
Start: 1940-03-01 00:00:00
End: 2026-08-01 00:00:00

Aligning all 15 Stations¶

In [13]:
station_ids = sorted(nz_monthly_pd["ID"].unique())

# Create every combination of station and month
full_index = pd.MultiIndex.from_product(
    [station_ids, full_months],
    names=["ID", "YEAR_MONTH"]
)

# Reindex the data to the complete timeline
nz_monthly_aligned = (
    nz_monthly_pd
    .set_index(["ID", "YEAR_MONTH"])
    .reindex(full_index)
    .reset_index()
)

print("Aligned dataset shape:", nz_monthly_aligned.shape)

nz_monthly_aligned.head()

Creating 15 subplots¶

In [14]:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Get the station IDs in a consistent order
station_ids = sorted(
    nz_monthly_aligned["ID"].unique()
)

# Create 5 x 3 subplot layout
fig, axes = plt.subplots(
    nrows=5,
    ncols=3,
    figsize=(18, 20),
    sharex=True,
    sharey=True
)

# Flatten the axes so we can loop through them
axes = axes.flatten()

for ax, station_id in zip(axes, station_ids):

    station_data = nz_monthly_aligned[
        nz_monthly_aligned["ID"] == station_id
    ]

    ax.plot(
        station_data["YEAR_MONTH"],
        station_data["TMIN"],
        label="TMIN"
    )

    ax.plot(
        station_data["YEAR_MONTH"],
        station_data["TMAX"],
        label="TMAX"
    )

    ax.set_title(station_id)
    ax.set_ylabel("Temperature (°C)")
    ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)

# Put legend on each subplot
for ax in axes:
    ax.legend(fontsize=8)

# Common x-axis label
fig.supxlabel("Year")

# Overall figure title
fig.suptitle(
    "Monthly Average TMIN and TMAX for New Zealand Stations",
    fontsize=16
)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Replotting using 12-month rolling average¶

In [15]:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, axes = plt.subplots(
    nrows=5,
    ncols=3,
    figsize=(18, 20),
    sharex=True,
    sharey=True
)

axes = axes.flatten()

for ax, station_id in zip(axes, station_ids):

    station_data = (
        nz_monthly_aligned[
            nz_monthly_aligned["ID"] == station_id
        ]
        .sort_values("YEAR_MONTH")
        .copy()
    )

    # 12-month rolling averages
    station_data["TMIN_SMOOTH"] = (
        station_data["TMIN"]
        .rolling(window=12, min_periods=12)
        .mean()
    )

    station_data["TMAX_SMOOTH"] = (
        station_data["TMAX"]
        .rolling(window=12, min_periods=12)
        .mean()
    )

    ax.plot(
        station_data["YEAR_MONTH"],
        station_data["TMIN_SMOOTH"],
        label="TMIN"
    )

    ax.plot(
        station_data["YEAR_MONTH"],
        station_data["TMAX_SMOOTH"],
        label="TMAX"
    )

    ax.set_title(station_id)
    ax.set_ylabel("Temperature (°C)")
    ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
    ax.legend(fontsize=8)

fig.supxlabel("Year")
fig.supylabel("Temperature (°C)")

fig.suptitle(
    "12-Month Rolling Average TMIN and TMAX for New Zealand Stations",
    fontsize=16,
    y=0.995
)

plt.tight_layout(rect=[0, 0, 1, 0.98])
plt.show()

What the figure shows

A few useful observations:

  1. The TMAX line is consistently above TMIN, as expected.
  2. Stations have noticeably different temperature levels, reflecting their different locations.
  3. Some stations have much shorter periods of available data than others.
  4. There are clear gaps in several station records, and these have been preserved rather than filled with artificial values.
  5. The 12-month smoothing removes most of the strong month-to-month seasonal oscillation and makes longer-term changes easier to compare.
  6. Using the same x- and y-axis scales across the subplots makes the stations directly comparable.

One methodological point for report

The observations were aggregated to monthly averages and then smoothed using a 12-month rolling mean. This reduced the strong short-term seasonal variation and made longer-term patterns between stations easier to compare. Missing observations were retained as gaps rather than being interpolated, so the visualisation does not imply data was available when it was not. All stations were aligned to the same monthly time axis and plotted using common temperature and time scales. That directly addresses all three things the question asks you to consider:

  1. Smoothing: monthly aggregation + 12-month rolling average
  2. Gaps: retained as missing values
  3. Alignment: common time and temperature scales

Ploting country-wide TMIN and TMAX¶

In [18]:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(16, 8))

ax.plot(
    country_monthly["YEAR_MONTH"],
    country_monthly["TMIN_SMOOTH"],
    label="TMIN"
)

ax.plot(
    country_monthly["YEAR_MONTH"],
    country_monthly["TMAX_SMOOTH"],
    label="TMAX"
)

ax.set_title(
    "12-Month Rolling Average TMIN and TMAX for New Zealand",
    fontsize=16
)

ax.set_xlabel("Year")
ax.set_ylabel("Temperature (°C)")

ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
ax.legend()

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

The country-wide time series shows that TMAX remains consistently higher than TMIN throughout the period. After the early part of the record, both series show noticeable variation over time, but the overall pattern suggests a gradual increase in temperatures in the later part of the dataset. The TMIN series generally stays around 7–10°C, while TMAX is mostly between about 15–19°C. There are also several shorter-term increases and decreases, particularly from the 1990s onwards. The 12-month rolling average makes these longer-term patterns easier to see by reducing the strong seasonal variation that would otherwise dominate the plot.

Extracting the year and aggregating¶

In [26]:
from pyspark.sql.functions import substring, avg

rainfall_year_country = (
    prcp_country
    .select(
        "COUNTRY_NAME",
        substring(col("DATE"), 1, 4).alias("YEAR"),
        "VALUE"
    )
    .groupBy("YEAR", "COUNTRY_NAME")
    .agg(
        avg("VALUE").alias("AVG_DAILY_RAINFALL")
    )
    .orderBy("YEAR", "COUNTRY_NAME")
)

Date: 22 June 2000

Interpretation

The maximum is not a sensible representation of Equatorial Guinea's average daily rainfall for 2000, because the country-year estimate is based on only one precipitation observation. While 436.1 mm of rainfall on a single day can occur as an extreme rainfall event, using that one observation as the annual average gives a highly misleading result. This demonstrates how sparse observations can create extreme country-year averages.

Question 2: Part (b)¶

In [70]:
# Verify the raw daily dataset used for Q2(a)

raw_daily_count = daily_all.count()

print("Raw daily records used:", raw_daily_count)
print("Approximately 3.19 billion:", raw_daily_count == 3190161793)

[Stage 86:=====================================================>(107 + 1) / 108]
Raw daily records used: 3190161793
Approximately 3.19 billion: True
In [71]:
prcp_count = (
    daily_parsed
    .filter(col("ELEMENT") == "PRCP")
    .count()
)

print("Raw daily records:", raw_daily_count)
print("PRCP observations:", prcp_count)

[Stage 89:=====================================================>(107 + 1) / 108]
Raw daily records: 3190161793
PRCP observations: 1095197420

Importantly, 17,789 is not being produced from a small subset of the dataset. The aggregation starts from the full 3.19 billion raw daily records, then selects the ~1.095 billion precipitation observations. The logic is therefore:

3,190,161,793 daily observations
              │
              ▼
        Parse daily data
              │
              ▼
     Filter ELEMENT = PRCP
              │
              ▼
      1,095,197,420 PRCP
              │
              ▼
   Group by YEAR + COUNTRY_NAME
              │
              ▼
          17,789 rows

Azerbaijan's 2025 average daily rainfall is 540 mm, but this value is based on only three reported precipitation observations, including one unusually high observation of 1220 mm. Therefore, the country-level value has very limited representativeness and is likely to act as an influential outlier in the choropleth.

One important methodological point

We should be precise about what our current AVG_DAILY_RAINFALL represents.

Our calculation is effectively:

all PRCP observations
        ↓
group by YEAR + COUNTRY
        ↓
average VALUE

Therefore, it is an average of reported PRCP observations, not necessarily an average of one daily rainfall value per calendar day. That's important because countries with lots of stations/reporting days contribute many observations, while countries like Liberia contribute only one. We should not change the Q2(a) result now, because that's the result we've already generated and saved. But for Q2(b), we absolutely need to acknowledge this limitation when discussing the outlier and the choropleth.

Checking how many countries have extremely sparse data?¶

In [31]:
# Check how many countries have very few observations in 2025

from pyspark.sql.functions import when, col, sum

country_2025_counts.groupBy().agg(
    (sum(when(col("count") <= 3, 1).otherwise(0))).alias("countries_1_to_3"),
    (sum(when(col("count") <= 10, 1).otherwise(0))).alias("countries_1_to_10"),
    (sum(when(col("count") <= 30, 1).otherwise(0))).alias("countries_1_to_30")
).show()

[Stage 36:=====================================================>(107 + 1) / 108]
+----------------+-----------------+-----------------+
|countries_1_to_3|countries_1_to_10|countries_1_to_30|
+----------------+-----------------+-----------------+
|               5|                9|               17|
+----------------+-----------------+-----------------+

Report Point

The 2025 rainfall estimates have highly uneven observational coverage. Five countries have three or fewer PRCP observations, and 17 have 30 or fewer. Consequently, extreme values based on very few observations, such as Azerbaijan's 540 mm/day estimate from only three observations, should be interpreted cautiously.

Creating ISO Codes dataframe¶

In [51]:
from pyspark.sql.types import StructType, StructField, StringType

mapping_rows = [
    (country, iso3)
    for country, iso3 in country_to_iso3.items()
]

mapping_schema = StructType([
    StructField("COUNTRY_NAME", StringType(), False),
    StructField("ISO3", StringType(), False)
])

country_mapping = spark.createDataFrame(
    mapping_rows,
    schema=mapping_schema
)

# Show the country names associated with duplicate ISO-3 codes

(
    rainfall_2025_iso
    .join(
        duplicate_iso3.select("ISO3"),
        on="ISO3",
        how="inner"
    )
    .select("COUNTRY_NAME", "ISO3", "AVG_DAILY_RAINFALL")
    .orderBy("ISO3", "COUNTRY_NAME")
    .show(truncate=False)
)

+------------------+----+------------------+
|COUNTRY_NAME      |ISO3|AVG_DAILY_RAINFALL|

|Jan Mayen [Norway]|SJM |15.602739726027398|
|Svalbard [Norway] |SJM |7.713656387665198 |
+------------------+----+------------------+

Report Point

Jan Mayen and Svalbard were represented separately in the dataset but both mapped to the same ISO-3 code (SJM). Since this creates an ambiguous geographic mapping for a country-level choropleth, these two records were excluded from the map rather than arbitrarily assigning one rainfall value to the shared code.

Removing the ambigous Jan Mayen [Norway] & Svalbard [Norway]¶

In [60]:
# Remove the ambiguous Svalbard/Jan Mayen mapping only for the choropleth

rainfall_2025_map = (
    rainfall_2025_iso
    .filter(~col("ISO3").isin(["SJM"]))
)

print("Records before removing SJM:", rainfall_2025_iso.count())
print("Records used for map:", rainfall_2025_map.count())
print("Unique ISO3 codes for map:", rainfall_2025_map.select("ISO3").distinct().count())

Find countries with stations but no 2025 rainfall¶

In [61]:
# Countries represented in the station metadata
station_countries = (
    stations
    .select("COUNTRY_NAME")
    .where(col("COUNTRY_NAME").isNotNull())
    .distinct()
)

# Countries with 2025 rainfall observations
rainfall_countries_2025 = (
    rainfall_2025_iso
    .select("COUNTRY_NAME")
    .distinct()
)

# Countries with stations but no 2025 rainfall observations
countries_no_2025_rainfall = (
    station_countries
    .join(
        rainfall_countries_2025,
        on="COUNTRY_NAME",
        how="left_anti"
    )
    .orderBy("COUNTRY_NAME")
)

print(
    "Countries with stations but no 2025 rainfall:",
    countries_no_2025_rainfall.count()
)

countries_no_2025_rainfall.show(

In [27]:
from pyspark.sql.functions import col, avg

rainfall_year_country_mm = (
    daily_parsed
    .filter(col("ELEMENT") == "PRCP")
    .withColumn("PRCP_MM", col("VALUE") / 10.0)
    .withColumn("YEAR", col("DATE").substr(1, 4))
    .join(
        stations.select("ID", "COUNTRY_NAME"),
        on="ID",
        how="inner"
    )
    .groupBy("YEAR", "COUNTRY_NAME")
    .agg(
        avg("PRCP_MM").alias("AVG_DAILY_RAINFALL_MM")
    )
)

rainfall_year_country_mm.show(10, truncate=False)

Extracting the correct rainfall dataset¶

In [12]:
# Extract corrected 2025 rainfall data
from pyspark.sql.functions import create_map, lit
from pyspark.sql.functions import col, avg


rainfall_2025_mm = (
    rainfall_year_country_mm
    .filter(col("YEAR") == "2025")
)

# Add ISO3 country codes using the mapping created earlier
rainfall_2025_iso = (
    rainfall_2025_mm
    .withColumn(
        "ISO3",
        create_map(
            *[x for pair in country_to_iso3.items() for x in (lit(pair[0]), lit(pair[1]))]
        )[col("COUNTRY_NAME")]
    )
)

rainfall_2025_iso.select(
    "COUNTRY_NAME",
    "ISO3",
    "AVG_DAILY_RAINFALL_MM"

# Create map-specific dataset

Creating the choropleth¶

In [22]:
import plotly.express as px
from pyspark.sql.functions import when, lit

# 95th percentile used only to control the visual colour scale
VIS_MAX = percentiles[4]

# Create plotting values.
# The original rainfall value is retained.
rainfall_2025_plot = (
    rainfall_2025_map
    .withColumn(
        "PLOT_RAINFALL_MM",
        when(
            col("AVG_DAILY_RAINFALL_MM") > VIS_MAX,
            lit(VIS_MAX)
        ).otherwise(col("AVG_DAILY_RAINFALL_MM"))
    )
)

# Convert the small country-level dataset to Pandas for Plotly
rainfall_2025_plot_pd = (
    rainfall_2025_plot
    .select(
        "COUNTRY_NAME",
        "ISO3",
        "AVG_DAILY_RAINFALL_MM",
        "PLOT_RAINFALL_MM"
    )
    .toPandas()
)

fig = px.choropleth(
    rainfall_2025_plot_pd,
    locations="ISO3",
    color="PLOT_RAINFALL_MM",
    hover_name="COUNTRY_NAME",
    hover_data={
        "ISO3": True,
        "AVG_DAILY_RAINFALL_MM": ":.2f",
        "PLOT_RAINFALL_MM": False
    },
    locationmode="ISO-3",
    color_continuous_scale="YlGnBu",
    range_color=(0, VIS_MAX),
    title="Average Daily Rainfall by Country, 2025",
    labels={
        "PLOT_RAINFALL_MM": "Average Daily Rainfall (mm/day)",
        "AVG_DAILY_RAINFALL_MM": "Actual Average (mm/day)"
    }
)

fig.update_layout(
    geo=dict(
        showframe=False,
        showcoastlines=True,
        projection_type="natural earth"
    )
)

fig.show()

Finalizing map annotation¶

In [24]:
fig.update_layout(
    title={
        "text": (
            "Average Daily Rainfall by Country, 2025"
            "<br><sup>"
            "Colour scale capped at the 95th percentile (11.25 mm/day); "
            "actual values are retained"
            "</sup>"
        ),
        "x": 0.5,
        "xanchor": "center"
    }
)

fig.show()

Report Point

The 2025 rainfall values were strongly right-skewed, with a median of 3.83 mm/day and a maximum of 54.0 mm/day. To improve visual differentiation among most countries, the choropleth colour scale was capped at the 95th percentile (11.25 mm/day). This was applied only to the visual colour scale, while the original rainfall values were retained. Countries without 2025 observations were treated as missing rather than zero.

One important interpretation¶

The map shows that rainfall varies substantially across countries in 2025, with higher average daily rainfall generally visible across parts of South/Southeast Asia, Central Africa and some tropical regions, while much lower values occur across many arid and semi-arid regions.

However, we should be careful about interpreting the map as a direct climate comparison because observation coverage is uneven. Some countries have no 2025 rainfall observations, while some of the high values may be based on relatively few observations.

The Azerbaijan result is a particularly good example: 54 mm/day is the maximum, but the 99th percentile is also 54 mm/day, showing how strongly the distribution is influenced by the extreme upper value.

Making the hover over information explicit¶

In [25]:
fig.update_traces(
    hovertemplate=(
        "<b>%{hovertext}</b><br>"
        "ISO3: %{customdata[0]}<br>"
        "Actual average rainfall: %{customdata[1]:.2f} mm/day"
        "<extra></extra>"
    ),
    customdata=rainfall_2025_plot_pd[
        ["ISO3", "AVG_DAILY_RAINFALL_MM"]
    ].values
)

fig.show()

Saved choropleth to:
rainfall_2025_choropleth.html

Report Interpretation¶

The choropleth shows the average daily rainfall for 2025 across countries with available observations. ISO3 country codes were used to match the rainfall data with the geographic boundaries. There were 172 country/territory records and all of them could be matched to an ISO3 code. Svalbard and Jan Mayen were excluded from the map because they shared the same SJM code, which could not uniquely represent both locations on the map. This exclusion was only applied to the visualisation and did not change the underlying rainfall data.

The rainfall values were strongly right-skewed. The median average daily rainfall was 3.83 mm/day, while the maximum was 54.0 mm/day for Azerbaijan. To make differences between most countries easier to see, the map colour scale was capped at the 95th percentile of 11.25 mm/day. The actual rainfall values were retained, so this cap only affects the colour representation of the map. Countries with no 2025 observations were treated as missing rather than zero rainfall.

The map shows generally higher rainfall values across several tropical regions, particularly parts of Africa, South and Southeast Asia and South America, while lower values are visible across many drier regions. However, the results should be interpreted with some caution because observation coverage is not consistent between countries. In particular, 47 countries or territories with stations had no rainfall observations available for 2025.
